findings.subsystem: oracle-relayer (neo-morpheus-oracle/workers/morpheus-relayer): fulfillment/callback delivery, retry/backoff, idempotency, durable queue + DLQ, block/request cursor scan, error classification
findings.title: Neo N3 fulfill confirmation timeout silently records request as fulfilled, permanently losing the callback
findings.evidence: neo-n3.js:964-992 confirmNeoN3FulfillExecution() degrades a tx whose application log never appears before the timeout to {vm_state:'UNKNOWN'} and RESOLVES instead of throwing. fulfillNeoN3Request() (neo-n3.js:1051-1058) returns that outcome normally. Crucially, processEvent (fulfillment.js:1085-1105) records the event as 'fulfilled'/'failed' based on prepared.success (the worker result) and NEVER inspects vm_state — grep confirms nothing downstream reads vm_state. It then calls clearRetryItem + recordProcessedEvent. If the fulfillRequest tx was dropped from the mempool (broadcast accepted by one node, never mined), the on-chain request stays Pending forever but the relayer has marked it processed. The request-cursor reconciliation path that could re-discover it (reconcilePendingRequests -> filterNewEvents -> hasProcessedEvent, request-processor.js:54-57) now skips it because it is in processed_records. The only external safety net, deploy/evm/callback-monitor.mjs, is Neo X (NEOX_NET) only and does not cover Neo N3. Net: a dropped fulfill tx on Neo N3 = a permanently unfulfilled user request with no retry and no alert.
findings.fix: In confirmNeoN3FulfillExecution, do not treat UNKNOWN as a benign terminal state. Either (a) throw a transient error ('fulfillRequest confirmation timed out') so classifyError routes it to scheduleCallbackRetry and a later attempt re-broadcasts (re-broadcast is idempotent: a landed tx FAULTs 'already fulfilled' -> settled), matching the Neo X path which throws on waitForNeoXReceipt timeout (neox.js:341-358); or (b) before recording fulfilled, re-read getRequest and confirm fulfilledAt/result is set on-chain, and if not, schedule a callback retry. Option (a) is the smaller, consistent change.
findings.risk: Moderate: changes a currently-tolerated 'best effort' path to a retrying one. Re-broadcast must rely on the existing isAlreadyFulfilledError->settled handling (present, fulfillment.js:1149-1160) to avoid double-finalize; under genuinely un-indexable-but-landed txs this adds one redundant retry that then settles. Reversible via the existing fulfillConfirmTimeoutMs knob.

findings.subsystem: oracle-relayer (neo-morpheus-oracle/workers/morpheus-relayer): fulfillment/callback delivery, retry/backoff, idempotency, durable queue + DLQ, block/request cursor scan, error classification
findings.title: Durable idempotency claim is bypassed during Supabase quota/outage backoff, allowing double-delivery across instances
findings.evidence: claimDurableJobForProcessing (queue.js:303-309) returns true unconditionally when shouldSkipSupabasePersistence() is active: `if (shouldSkipSupabasePersistence()) return true;`. The documented real outage cause for this system is exactly Supabase going over its size quota and returning 402 (memory: Oracle Supabase quota), which markSupabasePersistenceUnavailable latches into a 5-minute backoff (persistence.js:91-99, default MORPHEUS_SUPABASE_BACKOFF_MS=300000). During that whole window the cross-instance claim (the entire point of claimed_by/claimRelayerJob, queue.js:317-346) is disabled and every instance falls back to local-only state. Two relayer instances would then both process and both broadcast fulfillRequest for the same request. On-chain the second FAULTs 'already fulfilled' (handled as settled), so funds are safe, but it wastes a full GAS network fee per duplicate and emits a spurious failure path. Current prod runs a single morpheus-relayer.service (deploy/systemd), so this is latent rather than active today.
findings.fix: When durableQueue.enabled and persistence is in backoff, do not silently grant the claim. Either keep failClosed semantics (skip processing this tick, let the durable claim resume when Supabase returns) for multi-instance deploys, or gate the unconditional-true on an explicit single-instance flag (e.g. config.durableQueue.allowLocalClaimDuringBackoff). At minimum increment a metric and warn so an operator sees that idempotency protection is off, instead of returning true with no signal.
findings.risk: Low. If a single instance is deployed (current state) behavior is unchanged when the flag defaults to allow-local. The conservative (skip) path only changes behavior during a Supabase outage, which is already degraded.
findings.risk_note: Severity hinges on whether >1 relayer instance ever runs concurrently; only one systemd unit found, so kept at medium.

findings.subsystem: oracle-relayer (neo-morpheus-oracle/workers/morpheus-relayer): fulfillment/callback delivery, retry/backoff, idempotency, durable queue + DLQ, block/request cursor scan, error classification
findings.title: Mainnet block_cursor scan does a getapplicationlog RPC for every transaction in every scanned block (no pre-filter)
findings.evidence: scanNeoN3OracleRequestBlock (neo-n3.js:389-419) reads getblock then, for EVERY transaction in the block, calls getapplicationlog(txHash) (line 396) and only afterward filters notifications by contract (line 404: `if (strip0x(notification.contract) !== targetContract) continue`). There is no way on Neo N3 to know which txs touched the oracle contract without the app log, but the cost is unbounded: per tick the relayer scans up to maxBlocksPerTick=250 blocks (config.js:301), and mainnet defaults to scanMode='block_cursor' (config.js:435-437) — so the per-tick RPC fan-out is 250 getblock + (sum of all txs across 250 blocks) getapplicationlog calls, dominated by oracle-unrelated traffic. On a cold start or after downtime (cursor far behind) this multiplies, and against rate-limited public RPCs (rpcUrls failover) it can stall the loop. Testnet sidesteps this with n3index_notifications (single indexer query, neo-n3.js:443-497).
findings.fix: Prefer the indexer/notification path on mainnet too (make scanMode default 'n3index_notifications' or 'request_cursor' for mainnet, as Neo X already uses request_cursor by default, config.js:487). request_cursor (scanNeoN3OracleRequestsById) reads getRequest per id over [from,to] which is bounded by request volume, not total chain tx volume, and already skips settled requests (neo-n3.js:261-263). If block_cursor must stay, cap maxBlocksPerTick lower for it and document the RPC amplification.
findings.risk: Low-medium: switching the default mainnet scan mode changes the discovery source; request_cursor/n3index modes are already exercised and the cursor-reset guards (resolveRequestCursor) handle the transition. Reversible via MORPHEUS_RELAYER_NEO_N3_SCAN_MODE.

findings.subsystem: oracle-relayer (neo-morpheus-oracle/workers/morpheus-relayer): fulfillment/callback delivery, retry/backoff, idempotency, durable queue + DLQ, block/request cursor scan, error classification
findings.title: Single getLatestRequestId FAULT/transport error aborts the entire tick before due retries run (request_cursor mode)
findings.evidence: processChainByRequestCursor (request-processor.js:224) calls `const latestRequestId = await options.getLatestRequestId(config)` before runDueRetries. getNeoN3LatestRequestId throws on FAULT or RPC failure (neo-n3.js:221-231), and there is no try/catch around the call inside processChain* — the throw propagates to runRelayerOnce -> runRelayerLoop's catch (relayer.js:254-262) which logs and sleeps a full pollIntervalMs. The consequence: when getTotalRequests is temporarily unavailable (RPC hiccup), already-prepared callback retries that are DUE (including callback_pending redeliveries holding a signed fulfillment) are NOT attempted this tick even though they require no fresh scan. The retry path is starved by an unrelated discovery-RPC failure. Same shape for the block-cursor path via getLatestBlock (request-processor.js:140).
findings.fix: Run due retries independently of fresh discovery: wrap the discovery RPC (getLatestRequestId/getLatestBlock + scan) in a try/catch that logs and continues to runDueRetries, or call runDueRetries first. The retry queue is local/durable state that does not need a successful chain-tip read to drain.
findings.risk: Low. Decoupling retries from discovery only adds attempts; idempotency (already-fulfilled->settled) covers any double work. No cursor is advanced on the failed-discovery branch.

findings.subsystem: oracle-relayer (neo-morpheus-oracle/workers/morpheus-relayer): fulfillment/callback delivery, retry/backoff, idempotency, durable queue + DLQ, block/request cursor scan, error classification
findings.title: Dead-letter and durable job records embed the full original event, growing local state and Supabase rows unboundedly per request
findings.evidence: recordProcessedEvent pushes the entire `event` object (including payloadText, which for confidential.decrypt is an X25519 sealed envelope and for compute requests can be large) into chainState.dead_letters (state.js:263-275) and buildRelayerJobRecord stores the full `event` in the Supabase morpheus_relayer_jobs.event column (persistence.js:399). dead_letters is capped at deadLetterLimit (default 500, config.js:323) and processed_records at processedCacheSize (5000), so local state is bounded but each entry can be multi-KB. The Supabase jobs table has no such cap and was the system that already hit the 8GB quota (memory: Oracle Supabase quota). retry items also carry prepared_fulfillment (full result + signature) in both local state and worker_response.retry_meta, duplicated on every checkpoint/upsert.
findings.fix: Trim payloadText (and result_bytes_base64) to a bounded length or replace with a sha256 + length when persisting the event into dead_letters and Supabase job rows; keep the full payload only in the live retry item needed for redelivery. Consider a TTL/cleanup job for terminal (fulfilled/failed/exhausted) Supabase rows older than N days, given the documented quota incident.
findings.risk: Medium: manual replay (/api/relayer/dead-letters) reconstructs the event from the stored job; truncating payloadText would break replay of those requests. Replay must instead re-fetch the request from chain (getRequest) rather than rely on the stored payload, or keep payload only for non-terminal rows.

findings.subsystem: oracle-relayer (neo-morpheus-oracle/workers/morpheus-relayer): fulfillment/callback delivery, retry/backoff, idempotency, durable queue + DLQ, block/request cursor scan, error classification
findings.title: scheduleRetry/computeRetryDelayMs use deterministic exponential backoff with no jitter — synchronized retry storms
findings.evidence: Both backoff computations (state.js:297-300 scheduleRetry, fulfillment.js:109-111 computeRetryDelayMs) are `min(base * 2^(attempts-1), max)` with no random jitter. When a shared dependency fails (RPC outage, Nitro signer down, Supabase 402), every queued event fails at nearly the same time and is scheduled to the same next_retry_at buckets, so they all become due together and re-stampede the recovering dependency on the same tick (getDueRetryItems returns them all, request-processor.js:28-44, bounded only by maxRetryEventsPerTick). retryMaxDelayMs default is also low (10s, config.js:311-314), so buckets are coarse and collisions are frequent.
findings.fix: Add bounded jitter to the scheduled delay, e.g. delay = base*2^n then multiply by a random factor in [0.5,1.0] (full/equal jitter), in both computeRetryDelayMs and scheduleRetry. Keeps the cap but desynchronizes recovery.
findings.risk: Very low; only spreads retry timing. maxRetryEventsPerTick already provides a hard cap, so this is an incremental smoothing.

findings.subsystem: oracle-worker-edge (neo-morpheus-oracle: workers/nitro-worker + deploy/cloudflare edge + feed-pusher + emergency-vercel-runtime)
findings.title: Edge gateway returns no CORS headers, so browser consoles cannot fetch any tokenless GET lane
findings.evidence: deploy/cloudflare/morpheus-edge-gateway/worker.mjs has zero CORS handling: the default fetch() (lines 324-466), the json() helper from @neo-morpheus-oracle/shared/utils, the public-runtime routes (lines 341-376), and the worker handler (workers/nitro-worker/src/worker.js + platform/core.js json() at line 18) never set Access-Control-Allow-Origin and never answer an OPTIONS preflight. grep for 'Access-Control|cors|OPTIONS|preflight' across workers/nitro-worker/src, deploy/cloudflare, and packages/shared/src returns nothing. The platform consoles explicitly intend to call edge.meshmini.app GETs from the browser — apps/shared/components-react/ConsoleToolPanel.tsx:73-80 documents that tokenless GETs (feeds/price/:symbol, feeds/catalog, neodid/providers, oracle/public-key) are the only live lanes consoles should wire — but a cross-origin browser fetch from the host app to edge.meshmini.app is blocked by the same-origin policy with no ACAO header. This is the root cause of 'consoles cannot fetch live'.
findings.fix: In deploy/cloudflare/morpheus-edge-gateway/worker.mjs add a safe CORS layer scoped to the read-only, tokenless GET lanes: (1) handle request.method === 'OPTIONS' early with a 204 + Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, OPTIONS, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, and an allow-listed Access-Control-Allow-Origin (echo the request Origin only if it matches an env allow-list e.g. MORPHEUS_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS — meshmini host app + localhost dev); (2) on the cacheable GET responses (the CACHE_RULES set: health, providers, feeds/catalog, oracle/public-key, feeds/price) and the public-runtime routes, set the same Access-Control-Allow-Origin + Vary: Origin. Do NOT add wildcard CORS to the token/Turnstile-protected POST lanes. Add Vary: Origin so the CF cache does not serve one origin's ACAO to another.
findings.risk: Low/medium: additive, reversible. Must use an env allow-list (not '*') and add Vary: Origin to avoid cache poisoning of the ACAO header across origins; mistakes are config-level and reversible.

findings.subsystem: oracle-worker-edge (neo-morpheus-oracle: workers/nitro-worker + deploy/cloudflare edge + feed-pusher + emergency-vercel-runtime)
findings.title: Edge gateway makes origin fetches with no timeout — a hung origin stalls the worker (the exact Phala-outage failure mode)
findings.evidence: deploy/cloudflare/morpheus-edge-gateway/worker.mjs: the main proxy call originResponse = await fetch(originRequest) (line 428) and the two runtime-status probes readOriginRuntimeProbe → fetch(buildOriginProbeRequest(...)) (lines 303-305, invoked via Promise.all at 355-358) have no AbortSignal.timeout. grep for 'AbortSignal|timeout|signal' in worker.mjs returns nothing. By contrast every other fetch in the codebase caps duration (oracle/fetch.js fetchWithTimeout, feed-pusher AbortSignal.timeout(15000/25000), nitro-signer AbortSignal.timeout(10_000), providers.js Supabase 15_000). When the origin box hangs (precisely the degraded state described in the runtime catalog), the edge worker blocks until Cloudflare's wall-clock limit instead of failing fast to the existing 503 origin_unavailable path at lines 429-440.
findings.fix: Wrap each origin fetch with AbortSignal.timeout (e.g. an env MORPHEUS_EDGE_ORIGIN_TIMEOUT_MS default ~10s). For the proxy call, pass signal into fetch(originRequest, { signal }) and treat an AbortError the same as the existing catch → json(503, origin_unavailable). For the runtime-status probes, give each probe its own short timeout (~5s) so a hung /info or /health resolves to {ok:false,status:503} and the snapshot reports 'down' quickly instead of stalling Promise.all.
findings.risk: Low: pure timeout addition feeding the already-present 503 fallback path; reversible via env.

findings.subsystem: oracle-worker-edge (neo-morpheus-oracle: workers/nitro-worker + deploy/cloudflare edge + feed-pusher + emergency-vercel-runtime)
findings.title: VRF lane signs CSPRNG output without binding it to the request — replayable, not a true VRF
findings.evidence: workers/nitro-worker/src/oracle/vrf.js: handleVrf builds randomness via crypto.getRandomValues then signs ONLY { randomness } — const signed = await buildSignedResultEnvelope({ randomness }, payload). In chain/signing.js:197-198 the output_hash = sha256(stableStringify(result)), i.e. sha256({randomness}). The payload.request_id (and any caller seed/nonce) is returned in the JSON (vrf.js:11) but is NOT part of the signed bytes. Consequences: (1) the (randomness, signature, public_key) triple is not bound to any request, so a valid signed pair can be presented for a different request_id/round; (2) vrf_method:'csprng-signed' (vrf.js:19) is signed-RNG, not a verifiable random function — there is no proof the output is a deterministic function of a seed+key, so a malicious/compromised signer could grind outputs off-chain and pick a favorable one before signing. On-chain consumers (e.g. dice-game) that treat this as VRF inherit that trust assumption.
findings.fix: Include the request binding in the signed envelope: build the signed result over { request_id, seed/nonce, randomness, timestamp } so the signature commits to the specific request (stops cross-request replay). Document explicitly that this is 'TEE-attested signed randomness', not an unbiasable VRF, OR move to a real VRF construction (ECVRF) where the proof is verifiable and the output is deterministic from (seed, key). At minimum require and bind a caller-supplied nonce and reject reuse.
findings.risk: Medium: changing the signed payload shape changes output_hash/verification and must be coordinated with on-chain/consumer verification of the VRF lane; needs a versioned rollout.

findings.subsystem: oracle-worker-edge (neo-morpheus-oracle: workers/nitro-worker + deploy/cloudflare edge + feed-pusher + emergency-vercel-runtime)
findings.title: Emergency Vercel runtime shim is GET-only and 503s all real lanes — confirm it is wired as fallback, not the live origin
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/api/emergency-runtime/[...path]/route.ts only restores GET /health and GET /info (lines 85-90); every other path including the tokenless GET read lanes consoles depend on (feeds/price/:symbol, feeds/catalog, oracle/public-key, neodid/providers) returns json(503, runtime_temporarily_degraded) at lines 92-98, for all verbs. health() reports degraded:true / reason 'phala_runtime_control_plane_disabled' (lines 44-58). If the edge origin (MORPHEUS_*_ORIGIN_URL) ever points at this Vercel shim rather than the live nitro-worker box, then even the read lanes that the live box serves (per ConsoleToolPanel.tsx:76-79) collapse to 503 and consoles show preview-only — i.e. the shim is strictly less capable than the live worker for the read paths consoles actually use.
findings.fix: Either (a) extend the emergency shim to proxy/serve the safe read-only GET lanes (feeds/catalog, feeds/price/:symbol, oracle/public-key) so degraded mode still satisfies console reads, or (b) make absolutely sure the edge origin env vars point at the live box and the shim is only a documented manual break-glass. Add a runbook note + a checkly/health assertion that the active origin is NOT the emergency-vercel-runtime (the x-morpheus-runtime header already distinguishes them).
findings.risk: Low: changes are confined to a degraded-mode shim; extending it to read lanes is additive.

findings.subsystem: oracle-worker-edge (neo-morpheus-oracle: workers/nitro-worker + deploy/cloudflare edge + feed-pusher + emergency-vercel-runtime)
findings.title: Worker capability routing uses unanchored path.endsWith(), making route matching order-fragile
findings.evidence: workers/nitro-worker/src/capabilities.js resolveCapability (lines 315-326) matches via path.endsWith(route.match). Several capability paths are suffixes of others: '/providers' (id providers, line 177) is a suffix of '/neodid/providers' (id neodid_providers, line 137). It happens to work only because neodid_providers is registered earlier and first-match wins (Phase 1 loop). Any future reorder, or a new path that is an accidental suffix of an existing one, silently routes to the wrong handler. The comment at lines 124-127 acknowledges 'Order matters' but the safety relies entirely on hand-maintained ordering.
findings.fix: Match on the exact forwardedPath segment instead of endsWith: compare the normalized path (after stripping the mainnet/testnet prefix the edge already injects via x-morpheus-network) for equality against route.match, e.g. path === route.match || path.endsWith('/' + route.match.replace(/^\//,'')) anchored to a segment boundary. Keep the regex patterns for the genuine :param routes. This removes the ordering dependency and the neodid/providers vs providers ambiguity.
findings.risk: Medium: routing change touches every lane; must be covered by the existing capability tests before/after to prove no path regresses.

findings.subsystem: deploy-tooling (deploy/scripts: live-validate harness, contract deploy scripts, brittle frontend-structure snapshot tests, shared RPC libs)
findings.title: Stale runtime.modules in 4 migrated app manifests point host runtime panel at dead kernel methods
findings.evidence: apps/fogplay/neo-manifest.json, apps/gasbox/neo-manifest.json, apps/last-survivor/neo-manifest.json, apps/self-loan/neo-manifest.json each still declare runtime.modules with platform PlatformGame/PlatformDeFi and operations mapping to DEAD kernel methods (fogplay: placeCoinFlipBet/getCoinFlipBetLimits/getCoinFlipBet; gasbox: createGachaMachine/pullGacha/getGachaMachine; last-survivor: startCountdownRound/buyCountdownKeys/checkAndEndCountdownRound; self-loan: createLoan/repayLoan/addCollateral). These apps were migrated to self-contained standalone contracts (e.g. fogplay MiniAppCoinFlip 0x238488..., last-survivor MiniAppLastSurvivor 0xe238...) whose ABI has no such methods. dice-game, migrated correctly, has runtime: {}. The host SharedRuntimePanel renders operation buttons from runtime.modules.operations and dispatches those method names, so the host detail page exposes buttons that FAULT on the new contracts. The module's embedded networks.*.contract_hash is also stale (e.g. gasbox testnet 0x740671b1, self-loan testnet 0x39d4584d) and disagrees with the live standalone hashes.
findings.fix: Set runtime to {} in all four neo-manifest.json files (matching apps/dice-game/neo-manifest.json), since each app is now driven by its own ctx.services.chain wiring, not the shared SharedRuntimePanel kernel path. Add a deploy-scripts AST/manifest test asserting that any app whose default contract is a standalone MiniApp* contract carries no PlatformGame/PlatformDeFi runtime module (prevents regression).
findings.risk: Low. Removing dead module blocks only removes host-rendered buttons that already FAULT; no live contract or working flow depends on them. Verify each app still loads (it uses ctx.services.chain, not runtime modules).

findings.subsystem: deploy-tooling (deploy/scripts: live-validate harness, contract deploy scripts, brittle frontend-structure snapshot tests, shared RPC libs)
findings.title: Host contract-queries.ts holds pre-migration contract hashes + old-kernel decode coupling for 6 apps
findings.evidence: platform/host-app/lib/chain/contract-queries.ts CONTRACTS (line 11) and TESTNET_CONTRACTS (line 22) still hold pre-migration hashes: CONTRACTS.lastSurvivor=0xa7840a8d (the OLD shared PlatformGame mainnet hash, also reused for gasbox/fogplay), CONTRACTS.selfLoan=0x942da575, TESTNET_CONTRACTS.lastSurvivor=0x740671b1 (the OLD gasbox-module testnet hash, NOT the live standalone 0xe238516951...), TESTNET_CONTRACTS.selfLoan=0x39d4584d. PLATFORM_GAME_CONTRACT_HASHES (line 36) and the per-app switch (line 329 fogplay/gasbox/redenvelope) decode results assuming the old kernel ABI. The detail-page on-chain stats query therefore targets dead/wrong contracts and decodes with the wrong ABI for last-survivor/gasbox/fogplay/redenvelope/self-loan/platformAnchor.
findings.fix: Stop hand-maintaining CONTRACTS/TESTNET_CONTRACTS. The repo already generates apps/shared/constants/generated-miniapp-contracts.ts from the manifests (scripts/generate-miniapp-contract-registry.mjs, gated by lib/miniapp_contract_registry.test.mjs); import GENERATED_MINIAPP_CONTRACTS here so host hashes track the manifest single source of truth. Then rewrite the per-app decode branches to the new standalone ABIs (Rolled/Burned/getLoan-style reads) or drop on-chain stat decode for the migrated apps until rewritten. Add a test asserting contract-queries hashes equal the generated registry per network.

findings.subsystem: deploy-tooling (deploy/scripts: live-validate harness, contract deploy scripts, brittle frontend-structure snapshot tests, shared RPC libs)
findings.title: deploy_contract_neonjs.mjs computes a wrong predicted contract hash (passes raw hex string where a HexString is required)
findings.evidence: deploy/scripts/deploy_contract_neonjs.mjs:41 calls experimental.getContractHash(account.scriptHash, nef.checksum, manifest.name). neon-js helpers.js:224 getContractHash(sender,...) does new sc.ScriptBuilder().emit(ABORT).emitPush(sender).emitPush(nefChecksum).emitPush(contractName) and expects sender to be a u.HexString so emitPush pushes the 20 raw script-hash bytes. account.scriptHash is a plain hex STRING, so emitPush treats it as a UTF-8 string and pushes the ASCII bytes of the hex characters — producing a different script and a WRONG hash. That is exactly why line 116 (and the script's own header comment + deploy_contract_mainnet.mjs:13 'getContractHash is unreliable') always reports a mismatch. The proof it is a misuse not a neon bug: the Go path uses state.CreateContractHash (calc_contract_hashes.go:81, deploy_selected_miniapp_contracts.go:160) as authoritative for GetContractStateByHash + setOracle, and per project history mainnet==testnet hashes confirm the formula is correct. Real harm: line 74 uses the wrong expectedHash for the getContractState idempotency check, so an already-deployed contract is never detected and the script can re-deploy a duplicate.
findings.fix: Pass a HexString: experimental.getContractHash(pkg.u.HexString.fromHex(account.scriptHash), nef.checksum, manifest.name). Validate the fix by comparing the printed expected hash to deploy/scripts/calc_contract_hashes.go output for the same nef+deployer (must match). Keep the authoritative Deploy-notification readback as the source of truth but the idempotency precheck must use a correct prediction. Alternatively delete the local prediction entirely and gate idempotency on a supplied expectedHash argument (as deploy_contract_mainnet.mjs already does).
findings.risk: Low. One-line change; readback already overrides the prediction for the final RESULT_HASH, so the only behavior change is a correct idempotency precheck (strictly safer — avoids duplicate deploys).

findings.subsystem: deploy-tooling (deploy/scripts: live-validate harness, contract deploy scripts, brittle frontend-structure snapshot tests, shared RPC libs)
findings.title: 24 *_frontend_structure.test.mjs snapshot tests assert exact CSS/JSX source via regex; they drift on every redesign and gate CI
findings.evidence: deploy/scripts/lib has 24 *_frontend_structure.test.mjs (2789 lines); 19 assert pixel-exact CSS against raw source: e.g. dice_game_frontend_structure.test.mjs:82 grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 0.62fr) minmax(340px, 0.44fr), :107 min-height: 52px; red_envelope_frontend_structure.test.mjs:75 width: min(680px, 100%), :106 gap: 6px, :107 min-height: 44px, plus exact JSX literals like useState({ amount: "1". ci_workflow.test.mjs:25 confirms test:deploy-scripts runs on every push/PR, and verify_repo.sh runs it too. So any visual redesign (the 14-Jun timestamps show a redesign campaign already rewrote many of these) breaks the deploy-scripts CI gate — drift cost is real and recurring, and these tests assert presentation not behavior/contract correctness, which is out of scope for a deploy-scripts gate.
findings.fix: Replace the brittle regex-on-CSS layer with the parsed-AST / manifest approach this repo already uses elsewhere: miniapp_runtime_entrypoints.test.mjs parses TSX via the typescript dep (ts.createSourceFile, parseDiagnostics) and asserts behavioral facts (entrypoint resolves, registerAction wired, state shape) rather than CSS strings. Rewrite the frontend-structure tests to (a) parse the PlayArea/main TSX and assert the dispatch/registerAction/state contract + presence of named className roots, (b) assert no parse errors, and drop the exact grid-template-columns/min-height/px assertions. Keep only the high-value invariants (no fluid clamp, no radial gradient if that is a hard design rule) as coarse doesNotMatch guards. This makes the gate test behavior+contract, not pixels.
findings.risk: Low-medium. These are test files only; rewriting them cannot break runtime. Risk is losing some intentional design guardrails — mitigate by keeping the few genuine invariants and moving pure-visual assertions to the frontend visual-audit tooling instead of the deploy-scripts CI gate.

findings.subsystem: deploy-tooling (deploy/scripts: live-validate harness, contract deploy scripts, brittle frontend-structure snapshot tests, shared RPC libs)
findings.title: Five .mjs live validators duplicate the invoke/read/retry/confirm loop instead of using shared live_rpc.mjs, with divergent RPC defaults and no failover
findings.evidence: live_rpc.mjs (createLiveRpc) already provides invokeAndConfirm/readStack/nep17BalanceOf with retry + multi-endpoint failover, and is used cleanly by breakuppact/coinflip/dailycheckin/dicegame/govmerc/lastsurvivor/redenvelope/tarot/timecapsule (e.g. live_validate_breakuppact.mjs:18,29). But live_validate_burnleague.mjs:32-68, live_validate_tipjar.mjs:36-66, live_validate_selfloan_smoke.mjs:13-28, live_validate_withdraw.mjs, and live_validate_neo_message.mjs each re-implement ~50-70 lines of the same invoke()/read()/retry()/eventState()/gasBal() loop. They also hardcode a DIFFERENT default endpoint (NEO_TESTNET_RPC_URL || "https://rpc.t5.n3.nspcc.ru:20331") than the shared lib (lib/neo_network.js testnet default https://testnet1.neo.coz.io:443), so they cannot fail over and target a different node, causing inconsistent flakiness. Separately the .js flagship validators use a SECOND shared lib (lib/live_neo.js, which only provides decode + createWaitForLog), so there are two parallel RPC abstractions plus the 5 ad-hoc copies.
findings.fix: Migrate burnleague, tipjar, selfloan_smoke, withdraw, neo_message to import createLiveRpc from ./lib/live_rpc.mjs (replace their local invoke/read/retry with live.invokeAndConfirm/live.readStack/live.nep17BalanceOf), exactly as breakuppact/coinflip already do. Drop the hardcoded rpc.t5.n3.nspcc.ru default so they inherit neo_network.js resolution + NEO_RPC_ENDPOINTS failover. Longer term, fold live_neo.js's decode/event helpers into live_rpc.mjs (or have live_rpc re-export them) so the .js flagship validators and .mjs validators share one module, eliminating the dual-abstraction split.
findings.risk: Low. Validators are test/ops scripts, not production runtime; behavior is observable (run against testnet). live_rpc.mjs is fully injectable and unit-tested (live_rpc.test.mjs), so the swap is mechanical and the gate tests catch regressions.

findings.subsystem: cross-cutting-dataflow (contract-address single-source-of-truth, testnet/mainnet parity, kernel-vs-standalone classification, host→shared dependency direction)
findings.title: Host on-chain stats query the WRONG (dead kernel) contract: contract-queries.ts CONTRACTS/TESTNET_CONTRACTS diverge from the shared registry for 7 of 8 flagship apps
findings.evidence: platform/host-app/lib/chain/contract-queries.ts:11-31 hand-maintains CONTRACTS/TESTNET_CONTRACTS that are NOT imported from the shared generated registry (verified: the file has zero references to getMiniAppContractHash/MINIAPP_CONTRACTS/GENERATED). A programmatic diff vs apps/shared/constants/generated-miniapp-contracts.ts shows divergence for lastSurvivor, gasBox, fogPlay, selfLoan, redEnvelope (both nets) and platformAnchor (testnet) — 7/8 apps. e.g. host lastSurvivor mainnet=0xa7840a8d5404… (old PlatformGame kernel) vs registry=0x8e1e432e9663… (new standalone). verified.title: On-chain read paths never check invoke state===FAULT; reverts/wrong-ABI calls silently decode to zeros
verified.reason:
All four cited locations verified exactly as described. rpc-client.ts invokeRead (lines 74-81) returns the InvokeResult with no state check. pages/api/rpc/neo.ts (131-148) forwards upstream JSON verbatim with HTTP 200 whenever upstream.ok — a Neo invokefunction FAULT is valid JSON-RPC with no top-level error, so it passes as success (note: the separate /api/rpc/neo-read proxy DOES synthesize FAULT and its companion MiniAppLiveDataShared.invokeRead at line 20 checks state!=="HALT" — but the cited rpc-client/neo path does not). request-handler.ts invokeBridgeRead (60-66) only checks !response.ok || payload?.error, so a FAULT result is returned to the miniapp via reply({ok:true,result}). contract-queries.ts parseInteger:67 returns 0n for missing items and mapFromResult:117 returns {} for non-Map, so a FAULT (empty stack) decodes to zeros. The WIF write-path comparison is exactly correct: wif.ts:644-646 and 750-752 do `if (preflight.state && preflight.state !== "HALT") throw new Error(preflight.exception || ...)`. End-to-end confirmation: /api/miniapps/[appId]/live -> getLiveStatus -> getDoomsdayState -> invokeRead; on FAULT, res.stack[0] is undefined, mapFromResult -> {}, yielding jackpot "0"/playersOnline 0 returned as HTTP 200 with no error — indistinguishable from a genuine empty contract. So the defect is REAL as described.

Severity correction high -> medium: impact is read-only / display + observability. No funds move on a read, no security boundary is crossed, and every rpc-client invokeRead consumer already degrades to safe defaults (getContractStats and getLiveStatus wrap in try/catch; getSharedModeContractStats is called with .catch(()=>null); resolveSharedModeRuntime wraps its reads). The user-facing harm is showing false zeros and the bridge `call` returning fake-success to a miniapp (which already must tolerate empty reads). The finding's own evidence frames it as "plausible-but-false state," which is a correctness/error-masking issue, not a high-impact one. (Aside: an uncited but more material consequence exists — lib/miniapp-lifecycle.ts readCountdownLifecycleState does NOT check FAULT and feeds classifyCountdownLifecycle, where a FAULT -> {} -> roundId<=0 -> start_needed could trigger a spurious lifecycle write via the cron relayer; this strengthens that the bug is real but it's relayer-idempotent and not what the finding cited.)

Fix is correct and safe: throwing in invokeRead on non-HALT is backward-compatible because all read/display callers already catch; the cron lifecycle path has a top-level try/catch (the throw is contained and actually prevents the spurious start_needed write). The bridge throw is converted to reply({ok:false,error}) and read errors stay scoped to the miniapp UI (use-embedded-wallet-bridge.ts:124-132). Existing contract-queries.test.ts mocks the rpc-client module directly, so adding the check inside the real invokeRead does not break them.
verified.fix_correction: Minor hardening: mirror the write path's exact guard rather than a bare inequality — use `if (result.state && result.state !== "HALT") throw new Error(result.exception || `contract read faulted (state=${result.state})`)` so a (theoretically) absent state field does not throw, matching wif.ts:644/750. Optionally also add the same FAULT check to lib/chain/MiniAppLiveDataShared.invokeRead's sibling consumers and to readCountdownLifecycleState (lib/miniapp-lifecycle.ts) which currently feeds a FAULT-as-{} into the lifecycle classifier and can produce a spurious start_needed write. Keep the throw out of any path that does NOT already catch unless that caller is updated to handle it.

verified.title: N3Index apiFetch uses raw fetch with no timeout — hangs the deposit-confirmation poller for every payment flow
verified.reason: Verified against source. (1) apiFetch (n3index.ts:106) does `await fetch(url.toString())` with no AbortController/timeout. (2) No global fetch override/polyfill exists in the repo, so the runtime uses native browser fetch, which has NO default timeout — a stalled TCP connection hangs the await indefinitely. (3) The waitForTransactionStatus poll loop (n3index.ts:305-322) checks `Date.now() >= deadline` only at line 320, AFTER `await getContractEvents(...)` returns; a connection hung inside that await never returns control, so the deadline literally cannot fire. The loop is not timeout-bounded against a single hung request. (4) Call chain confirmed exactly: getContractEvents → waitForTransactionStatus → waitForDepositConfirmation (useContractInteraction.ts:87-100) → ChainService.prepayAndInvoke (ChainService.ts:578) AND invokeWithDirectPrepaidGas (useContractInteraction.ts:411), i.e. the deposit-then-act path of every migrated payment app, plus direct callers in custom-anchor, milestone-escrow, and quadratic-funding. (5) ChainService.withProcessing (289-300) holds isProcessing true (try/finally) until the awaited fn resolves — a hung poll freezes the write with isProcessing stuck true, bricking the UI until reload. (6) fetchWithTimeout exists (fetch-timeout.ts, AbortController-backed, DEFAULT 10s) and is already adopted by wallet-sdk-composables.ts; n3index is the outlier transport. Per project memory the N3Index/oracle infra has actually been degraded/down, so a stalled response is a realistic, not theoretical, scenario. Minor corroborating inaccuracies that do NOT affect the core defect: it is 3 apps that call waitForDepositConfirmation directly (not 4); the file useEvents.ts does not exist; and EdgeClient.ts timeout usage was not grep-confirmed.
verified.fix_correction: The proposed fix is correct and safe. Route apiFetch's fetch through fetchWithTimeout({ timeoutMs: 10_000 }). Crucially, apiFetch's `await fetch` is NOT wrapped in a try/catch (only res.text()/JSON.parse is), so a thrown FetchTimeoutError propagates cleanly to getContractEvents and is caught by the poll loop's `catch (e)` (n3index.ts:313), where it is handled exactly like an unreachable indexer: returns "unreachable" if no poll has yet succeeded (caller uses fixed-delay fallback), or continues to the deadline check and retries if already reachable. 10s timeout ≥ 3s default pollIntervalMs, so a normal slow response is not aborted mid-poll. No test regressions expected: the deposit-settle/ChainService tests inject confirmDeposit / mock waitForTransactionStatus / unstub global fetch rather than exercising the real apiFetch, and there is no dedicated n3index unit test that mocks raw fetch. One small refinement: ensure the chosen timeout stays >= pollIntervalMs for any non-default callers too (only ChainService/quadratic use the defaults today), and consider that on each retry iteration the 10s bound applies per-request, which is the desired bounded behavior.

verified.title: Gambling games (CoinFlip/DiceGame/GasBox) drainable via same-tx abort-on-loss — no anti-composition/commit-reveal guard
verified.fix_correction: Proposed fix (a) — the anti-contract guard — is INSUFFICIENT and would give a false sense of safety. The author's own viable mechanism reduces to `Runtime.CallingScriptHash == Runtime.EntryScriptHash` (plus a redundant `ContractManagement.GetContract(CallingScriptHash)==null`). That correctly blocks a *deployed wrapper contract* (its hash != EntryScriptHash). BUT the abort-on-loss attack does NOT require a deployed contract at all: an attacker can craft the transaction's OWN entry script to (1) GAS.transfer the bet credit, (2) call Flip/Roll, (3) read the returned outcome left on the eval stack, and (4) conditionally ABORT — all inside the single entry VM script. In that case CallingScriptHash == EntryScriptHash is TRUE, so guard (a) passes and the exploit still works. (Verified there is genuinely no EntryScriptHash/CallingScriptHash guard today; only CheckWitness(player) at CoinFlip.cs:135, DiceGame.cs:146, GasBox.cs:236; the wrapper passes CheckWitness by signing with WitnessScope.Global which propagates through intermediaries — the repo's legit path uses CalledByEntry, deploy/scripts/lib/live_rpc.mjs:144,190.) Therefore only fix option (b), commit/reveal split across two blocks, actually closes the hole: bet() records the wager + commit height in one tx; settle() in a LATER block reads Runtime.GetRandom at reveal time — the attacker cannot revert a future-block settlement they do not control and cannot predict a future block seed. Recommendation: implement (b) for all three (redeploy + frontend rewire), NOT (a). One refinement to the finding: GasBox/Pull has no win/lose binary (AddItem requires amount>0 so every pull pays a positive prize), so its variant is 'force-the-jackpot' — abort unless chosenIndex == the MaxPrize item — bounded per pull by (MaxPrize - Price) but still pool-draining; the contract's 'removes the abort-and-retry exploit' claim (GasBox.cs:35) is false. Until redeploy, the only real mitigation is keeping bankrolls/pools minimal (loss is bounded by funded bankroll, which the activation guards enforce).
verified.reason: CONFIRMED real. Read all three contracts in full. (1) The three settle the outcome atomically in the same tx as the bet and gate ONLY on Runtime.CheckWitness(player) — confirmed no EntryScriptHash/CallingScriptHash/GetContract anti-composition guard anywhere in the game contracts (grep returned none; the only such guards live in unrelated MiniApps). (2) CheckWitness(attacker_EOA) passes through an intermediary when the attacker signs with WitnessScope.Global (a free choice for any tx sender). (3) The flip/roll outcome is returned to the caller (Flip returns outcome, Roll returns rolled), so a same-tx caller can inspect it and ExecutionEngine.Assert(won) to revert the entire atomic invocation on a loss — undoing both the bet-credit deposit (OnNEP17Payment at CoinFlip.cs:114-121) and the bankroll += amount loss-leg, committing only winning bets. This deterministically defeats the 5%/edge math and drains the house bankroll/pool. The docstrings explicitly claiming 'a player cannot see it and abort — there is no abort-and-retry' (CoinFlip.cs:29-32, DiceGame.cs:33-37) and 'removes the abort-and-retry exploit' (GasBox.cs:35) are FALSE. Severity critical is justified: an unconditional, repeatable, zero-cost-on-failure economic break of deployed+funded mainnet contracts (per memory the 10 self-contained contracts incl. coinflip are live on mainnet with NR3E4D8N owner). Loss is bounded by the funded bankroll (activation/coverage guards prevent over-betting), and current funding is small (~2 GAS coinflip per memory), which caps present-day blast radius but does not reduce the class of the bug. The defect and root cause are accurately described; the disagreement is only with the proposed fix.

verified.title: GetRandom-based value-bearing games (CoinFlip/DiceGame/GasBox) are block-producer-biasable; player+Time+gameId mix adds no protection
verified.reason:
All code citations verified exactly. MiniAppCoinFlip.cs:156 (GetRandom), :158 (mix=player+Time+gameId), :160 (outcome=(entropy+mix)%2), :48 MAX_BET=100 GAS, :31 doc admits "NOT VRF-grade; a block producer has some influence". DiceGame.cs:168/:170 same pattern, :53 MAX_BET=20 GAS. GasBox.cs:252/:254 weighted draw paying a real NEO/GAS pool. Tarot.cs:126 and RedEnvelope.cs:198 confirmed. Core technical claims hold: (1) Neo N3 Runtime.GetRandom is a deterministic PRNG seeded by the block nonce chosen by the consensus speaker, so a consensus node, when it is the speaker, can grind the nonce and/or select which of its own bet txs land to bias 2-outcome (CoinFlip) and 6-outcome (Dice) games in its favor. (2) The player+Runtime.Time+gameId mix provides ZERO protection against a producer: player is the attacker's own address, gameId is a predictable counter, and Runtime.Time is the block timestamp the proposer also sets — all known/controllable, so the producer can pick a nonce making (entropy+mix)%2 == its choice. The mix only frustrates a non-producer front-runner, which is not the threat. The project's own DevPack (MiniAppMoneyBase.cs:113-116) states this is "not for adversarial high-value settlement", and a RandomnessLog (TEE-attested) contract exists but these standalone contracts deliberately bypass it because the oracle is down. So the defect is REAL as described.

Severity corrected high->medium: the attack is NOT permissionless — it requires being one of the ~7 elected dBFT consensus/committee nodes (high barrier), the bias is statistical/opportunistic (speaker only a fraction of blocks for its own bets), and total exposure is bounded by the small house bankroll (per project memory, mainnet CoinFlip bankroll was primed at ~2 GAS). The finding itself notes exposure is bankroll-bounded. Tarot (no payout) and RedEnvelope (only fairness of distributing the creator's own funds among claimers; no house loss) are correctly carved out as acceptable. This is a genuine trust-model/robustness weakness with a constrained actor and bounded loss — medium, not high.

Fix is only partially correct/safe: (a) The commit-reveal "see prior finding ... defeats the abort attack" cross-reference is inconsistent with these contracts — they already removed abort-and-retry by settling in the SAME tx as the wager (CoinFlip.cs:30-31, Dice.cs:35-36, GasBox.cs:35), so there is no abort attack here to fix; introducing cross-block commit-reveal would re-add a multi-tx/UX surface and, critically, does NOT fully defeat single-block-producer bias unless the reveal entropy comes from a source the future-block producer cannot grind (a naive future-GetRandom reveal is still grindable). The fix overstates that commit-reveal solves producer bias. (b) The VRF-oracle option is the genuinely correct fix but is NOT actionable today — the Morpheus signer is non-operational, which is the entire reason these standalone GetRandom contracts exist. (c) The MAX_BET cap reduces per-bet extraction but the real exposure ceiling is the bankroll (a producer can repeatedly win small bets up to it), so it is a partial mitigation only. (d) The UI-documentation recommendation is correct and has real value: the current UI (apps/fogplay/src/locale/messages.ts:46,57; apps/dice-game/src/locale/messages.ts:23,49,125-126 vrfTrustLine) talks up "Neo's native randomness ... for auditability" without disclosing the block-producer bias, i.e. it oversells fairness.
verified.fix_correction: Adopt only the actionable, no-regression parts and drop the misframed commit-reveal cross-reference. Concretely: (1) Lower CoinFlip MAX_BET from 100 GAS toward DiceGame's 20 GAS (or lower) so per-event extraction is small relative to producer block reward, and keep the house bankroll deliberately small — this bounds cumulative exposure, which the MAX_BET cap alone does not. (2) Add an honest UI disclosure on FogPlay and Dice that randomness is Neo's block-seeded GetRandom (not VRF), so a consensus node has some influence; remove/soften fairness-overselling copy (the dice vrfTrustLine and fogplay aboutBody). This is the highest-value, zero-blast-radius change and needs no redeploy. (3) Treat VRF-oracle integration as the real long-term fix, gated on restoring the Morpheus/RandomnessLog signer — do NOT present it as currently available. (4) If a code-level mitigation is pursued, prefer a true commit-reveal where the reveal entropy is sourced so the settling block's producer cannot grind it (e.g., combine a player-chosen secret committed in tx A with GetRandom revealed in a later block AND require the bettor — not the producer — to trigger reveal), rather than implying same-block GetRandom or any single future-block GetRandom defeats producer bias. Note this re-adds multi-tx UX and an (economically neutral for a wager) non-reveal/forfeit path, which the current same-tx design intentionally avoids — so it is a real tradeoff, not a strict improvement. Document the trust assumption regardless.

verified.title: SelfLoan: owner-set static price + no liquidation + no defaulted-collateral recovery makes the GAS pool default-exposed
verified.reason:
Code confirmed at cited lines. Borrow() (cs:196-200) values collateral as collateral*price where price is an owner-set static value with only a >0 check (SetNeoPrice cs:150-156); there is no oracle, no staleness/sanity bound, no interest, and no liquidation (cs:31-35). The only collateral-release path is the borrower's own full Repay() (cs:280-285) — there is NO owner/keeper/anyone path to seize a defaulted loan's locked NEO, so a defaulted loan freezes its NEO forever AND drains GAS from the pool with zero recourse. So the substance of the finding is real: under adverse price/misconfiguration a borrower who received GAS worth more than the real resale value of the locked NEO has no incentive to repay, and the pool eats an unrecoverable loss.

Two corrections to the finding:
1) FRAMING ERROR: the title says "undercollateralizable on NEO appreciation." That is inverted — appreciation makes the locked NEO worth MORE than the loan, which strengthens the repay incentive (pool-safe). The real default driver is NEO DEPRECIATION below the LTV ratio of the configured price, or an owner-set price that drifts/fat-fingers above market. The owner-error vector the finding also names is correct.
2) The finding overstates "drainable by design." At origination LTV<=40% (TIER3, cs:49) the borrower receives only 40% of the configured collateral value, i.e. is heavily over-collateralized at the set price; default is profitable only once real NEO value falls below ~40% of the configured price (or on owner misconfiguration). It is a tail/misconfiguration risk, not a routine drain.

SEVERITY high -> medium: loss is bounded by the funded GAS pool, which is deliberately tiny (memory + smoke scripts: mainnet primed pool 5 GAS @ price 3 GAS/NEO; testnet 2 GAS @ 5 GAS/NEO) — an MVP/demo desk, not a real market. Price and pool are owner-only and the same owner key already fully controls pool funds via WithdrawPool, so the "owner sets price too high" path is a self-inflicted error by the trusted party, not an external exploit. Real but bounded and mostly trust/config-gated => medium.

Context the finding misses: the README markets this as an Alchemix-style "self-repaying, zero-liquidation" loan, yet the contract implements NO yield-based auto-repayment (repayment is purely manual via repay()). So "no liquidation" is an intentional advertised design choice (weakening it as a pure defect) while the genuine gap is "no recovery for the pool / frozen defaulted NEO."

FIX: directionally correct and safe. The interim no-redeploy mitigation (small pool, conservative price) is already what's deployed and is safe. The structural liquidation fix is right but (a) directly contradicts the README's "zero liquidation, ever" selling point so it needs a product decision, and (b) requires redeploy + frontend rewire and careful discount/threshold design — the proposal acknowledges the redeploy/rewire cost and correctly bounds loss to the funded pool. Lower-effort fixes the proposal omits: add a price-change rate bound to SetNeoPrice, and add an owner path to seize a defaulted loan's locked NEO so the pool at least recovers the collateral.
verified.fix_correction: Two additions to the proposed fix: (1) Add an owner/keeper path to seize+release a defaulted loan's locked NEO collateral — without it, a default freezes the NEO forever AND loses pool GAS (the finding only addresses the GAS loss). (2) Add a max price-change-rate bound and/or a two-step price update in SetNeoPrice to guard the fat-finger vector cheaply without changing the no-liquidation product story. Note that adding a true liquidation path conflicts with the app's advertised "zero liquidation, ever" design and therefore needs a product decision, not just an engineering change.

verified.title: Neo N3 fulfill confirmation timeout silently records request as fulfilled, losing the callback (production request_cursor mode)
verified.reason:
DEFECT CONFIRMED, but the finding's described loss MECHANISM is partly wrong.

Verified true:
- confirmNeoN3FulfillExecution (neo-n3.js:983-989) degrades a tx whose app log never appears before the 45s timeout to {vm_state:'UNKNOWN'} and RESOLVES (does not throw).
- fulfillNeoN3Request (neo-n3.js:1051-1058) returns that outcome normally; deliverPreparedFulfillment (fulfillment.js:444-468) returns {...prepared, fulfill_tx}, so result.success == prepared.success (the WORKER result). processEvent (fulfillment.js:1085-1104) records 'fulfilled'/'failed' from result.success and NEVER inspects vm_state. grep confirms vm_state is write-only — nothing downstream reads it. recordProcessedEvent then marks it processed and clearRetryItem drops any retry.
- Neo X correctly THROWS on confirmation timeout (waitForNeoXReceipt, neox.js:341-358) -> classifyError('timed out')='transient' -> retried. The N3 vs EVM asymmetry is real.
- deploy/evm/callback-monitor.mjs is Neo X only (NEOX_NET/NEOX_RPC, deploy/evm/); no Neo N3 safety net.
Net effect (dropped fulfill tx => request stays Pending on-chain forever, relayer marked it fulfilled, no retry, no alert) is REAL for the production scan mode.

Mechanism correction (the finding is inaccurate here):
- The finding blames reconcilePendingRequests -> filterNewEvents -> hasProcessedEvent skipping the request because it is in processed_records. That is WRONG for the default processChain modes (testnet n3index_notifications, mainnet block_cursor): the block-scan event key is chain:reqId:txHash:logIndex:height while the request-id reconciliation key (buildNeoN3EventFromRequestRecord sets txHash:'', logIndex:0, blockNumber:createdAtMs) is chain:reqId::0:createdAtMs. buildEventKey produces DIFFERENT keys (verified by direct computation), so hasProcessedEvent would NOT match and reconciliation WOULD re-discover the still-Pending request (the alreadySettled/hasOutcome guard at neo-n3.js:261-263 only filters genuinely settled ones) — i.e. reconciliation is actually a partial safety net in those modes.
- The ACTUAL production mode is request_cursor: render-nitro-compose-env.mjs:243-246 defaults MORPHEUS_RELAYER_NEO_N3_SCAN_MODE='request_cursor', and claudedocs/monorepo-review-2026-05-29.md states only request_cursor works end-to-end. In request_cursor mode processChainByRequestCursor (request-processor.js:201-260) has NO reconcilePendingRequests at all; the request id is permanently lost via forward-only cursor advancement (last_request_id = toRequestId), not via processed_records dedup. Same outcome, different code path than cited.

So the defect and conclusion are real (in production mode); the citation of the reconciliation/processed_records skip is the wrong loss path.
verified.fix_correction:
Fix option (a) is correct and safe. Make confirmNeoN3FulfillExecution throw on timeout (e.g. 'fulfillRequest confirmation timed out'): classifyError matches 'timed out' (fulfillment.js:94) -> 'transient' -> since preparedForRedelivery is set, processEvent routes to scheduleCallbackRetry (fulfillment.js:1177-1213) and a later tick re-broadcasts the prepared fulfillment. Idempotency holds: if the original tx actually landed, the re-broadcast FAULTs on the contract assert 'request already fulfilled' (MorpheusOracle.cs:925); assertNeoN3HaltExecution surfaces that message; isAlreadyFulfilledError matches 'already fulfilled' (fulfillment.js:53-59) -> recordTerminalOutcome status 'settled' (fulfillment.js:1149-1160). No double-finalize. Reversible via the existing fulfillConfirmTimeoutMs knob.

Recommended improvements to the writeup before/when fixing:
1. Correct the loss mechanism: the production-relevant path is request_cursor (no reconcile; loss via cursor advancement), not reconcilePendingRequests/hasProcessedEvent. Verify the deployed MORPHEUS_RELAYER_NEO_N3_SCAN_MODE; if a deployment runs block_cursor/n3index_notifications, the bug is masked by reconciliation re-discovery (different event key), so the impact is mode-dependent.
2. Tighten the throw vs UNKNOWN distinction: only throw when the broadcast was accepted but the log is unavailable; preserve the existing FAULT-throws-immediately behavior (already handled at neo-n3.js:977-980). Avoid retrying forever — the prepared-fulfillment lane is already capped by resolveCallbackRetryCeiling (fulfillment.js:121-125) and dead-letters permanent failures, so a genuinely un-indexable-but-landed tx settles on the next attempt rather than looping.
3. Optionally also (or instead) add a Neo N3 equivalent of callback-monitor.mjs (scan getRequest for long-Pending ids past the cursor) as a defense-in-depth alert.

verified.reason: Verified against source. claimDurableJobForProcessing (queue.js:303-308) returns true unconditionally when shouldSkipSupabasePersistence() is active, and this early-return at line 306-308 sits BEFORE the failClosed-honoring ensureDurableQueueAvailable check at line 309 — so during a quota backoff both the cross-instance claim (claimed_by/claimRelayerJob, queue.js:317-346) AND the configured failClosed safety are silently defeated. An existing test (queue.test.mjs:172-189) explicitly asserts claimed===true with failClosed:true during quota backoff, proving the bypass is current, intentional-looking behavior. Funds-safe claim is correct: isAlreadyFulfilledError (fulfillment.js:53-82) classifies the on-chain second-attempt fault as 'settled', so the only cost of a duplicate is a wasted GAS network fee plus a spurious failure path. Severity held at medium: the double-delivery itself requires >=2 request-processing relayers concurrently, which the current topology does NOT have (single morpheus-relayer container in deploy/nitro/docker-compose.yml; single deploy/systemd/morpheus-relayer.service; the split-relayer compose splits by MODE feed_only vs requests_only so still only one request-processing instance; no replicas/scale config found) — so the double-broadcast is latent, as the reviewer states. However medium remains defensible because a configured safety control (failClosed, default-true in prod per config.js:326) is silently defeated with zero operator signal during a recurring documented event (quota 402), which is a real robustness defect regardless of instance count. Low would also be defensible given latency; not below that.
verified.fix_correction: Fix is correct and safe; recommend implementing the minimal variant plus the gating flag. (1) At queue.js:306-308, instead of bare `return true`, emit a one-line warn + increment a metric (e.g. claim_idempotency_disabled_total) so the bypass is observable. Net: low regression risk as scoped.

Every console renders the preview-only branch (config.execute is undefined). So the documented intent is an aspiration in a comment, not shipped behavior.
3. The real live price path bypasses the edge entirely: apps/shared/composables/useMorpheusDataFeed.ts reads prices directly from the on-chain MorpheusDataFeed contract via Neo JSON-RPC ("No HTTP ... no edge proxy"). CORS is irrelevant to it.

verified.fix_correction: The proposed fix (env-allow-listed ACAO scoped to tokenless GET lanes + an OPTIONS 204 handler + Vary: Origin on cached responses, with no wildcard and no CORS on token/Turnstile POST lanes) is technically correct and safe. Adding Vary: Origin is the right cache-poisoning guard for caches.default. One caveat for whoever implements it: in worker.mjs the cacheable response is stored via cache.put(request, response.clone()) at lines 458-460 — a per-origin ACAO must NOT be written into the cached body, or the CF cache will serve origin A's ACAO to origin B even with Vary unless the cache key incorporates Origin; safest is to set ACAO AFTER reading from cache (decorate on the way out) rather than caching it, OR ensure Vary: Origin is part of the stored response so CF varies the cache entry. The fix description's "set the same ACAO on the cacheable GET responses ... add Vary: Origin" is acceptable as long as Vary is stored with the cached entry. Most importantly: this is an enabler, NOT a fix for a live bug — the consoles must ALSO wire the execute hook to a cross-origin GET for CORS to have any user-visible effect; without that wiring the change is inert.

verified.title: Edge gateway origin fetches lack request timeouts, breaking fast-fail on a hung origin
verified.reason: Code claims verified against deploy/cloudflare/morpheus-edge-gateway/worker.mjs. The fallback paths are present and correct: the proxy catch at 429-440 returns json(503, origin_unavailable), and the probe catch at 312-321 returns {ok:false,status:503}, which packages/shared/src/public-runtime.js getHealthState maps to 'down' -> snapshot status 'down' -> HTTP 503. So the fix's claim that a timed-out fetch feeds the already-present 503 path is logically sound. The codebase otherwise standardizes timeouts everywhere (feed-pusher AbortSignal.timeout 12000/15000/25000/60000; workers/nitro-worker AbortSignal.timeout 10_000/15_000 incl. nitro-signer, providers.js, fetch.js fetchWithTimeout; and notably the SIBLING worker deploy/cloudflare/morpheus-control-plane/lib/execution-plane.js implements fetchJsonWithTimeout default 30000ms, env-configurable), so the missing timeout in the edge gateway is a real inconsistency/gap, not an intentional design. The defect is genuine for the hung/slow-origin case: a hung origin makes the worker block until Cloudflare's wall-clock subrequest limit (~30s) and return a generic 524 instead of the fast structured 503 the code clearly intends; worse, /api/runtime/status — whose whole purpose is outage visibility — would itself hang instead of reporting 'down'. Minor evidence nit: fetchWithTimeout is at workers/nitro-worker/src/oracle/fetch.js, not 'oracle/fetch.js'. Fix is correct and safe: adding signal: AbortSignal.timeout(...) to each fetch is non-breaking against the existing test suite (worker.test.mjs mocks global.fetch and ignores init/signal), reversible via env, and routes AbortError into the existing 503 fallback. Map AbortError in the proxy catch (429-440) to the same 503 origin_unavailable (optionally include message: 'origin_timeout'); the probe catch (312-321) already returns {ok:false,status:503} which yields 'down', so no extra handling needed there. Make the timeout env-configurable (MORPHEUS_EDGE_ORIGIN_TIMEOUT_MS) consistent with the sibling control-plane worker's MORPHEUS_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_MS pattern. Adding signal to the fetches does not break the current node:test suite since it mocks global.fetch and ignores init/signal.

verified.title: VRF lane signs CSPRNG output without binding it to the request — replayable, not a true VRF
verified.reason:
The finding conflates two claims; its headline claim is refuted and the real residual is over-severitied.

CODE READS ACCURATELY: vrf.js handleVrf builds randomness via crypto.getRandomValues and signs only {randomness} (const signed = await buildSignedResultEnvelope({ randomness }, payload)). signing.js:197-198 confirms outputHash = sha256(stableStringify(result)) over {randomness}, and request_id is returned in JSON but not in the signed worker bytes. vrf_method:'csprng-signed' is correct.

CLAIM (1) CROSS-REQUEST REPLAY — REFUTED. The worker's csprng-signed envelope signature ({randomness} only) is an INTERNAL artifact that is NEVER verified on-chain. The actual on-chain trust anchor is the relayer/fulfiller-signed fulfillment digest, which already fully binds the request:
- EVM: MorpheusOracleEVM.sol fulfillRequest (lines 144-161) computes fulfillmentDigest = keccak256(abi.encode("morpheus-evm-fulfillment-v1", block.chainid, address(this), requestId, keccak(appId), keccak(moduleId), keccak(operation), success, keccak(result), keccak(error))) and requires ecrecover(ethSigned, signature) == oracleVerifier. So requestId + deployment (chainid+address) + identifiers + result are all bound.
- Neo N3: router.js buildFulfillmentDigestBytes (302-375) binds requestId + sha256(appId/moduleId/operation) + result + contract script hash + network magic. The comment at lines 298-300 explicitly states this binding "prevents an attacker from reusing a fulfillment signature meant for one (appId, moduleId, operation) tuple against a different request that shares the same requestId" — i.e. the exact threat the finding raises is already designed out at the verification layer. validate-vrf.mjs:56-82 shows the consumer-side reconstruction of this same request-bound digest. A signed (randomness, sig) pair therefore CANNOT be presented for a different request_id/deployment on-chain.

CLAIM (2) NOT A TRUE VRF / SIGNER CAN GRIND — CONFIRMED but LOW. grep across vrf.js + both contracts found zero seed/commit/nonce/blockhash/ECVRF/prevrandao mechanisms. csprng-signed is signed RNG, not a verifiable function of (seed, key), so a compromised oracle-verifier signer could grind getRandomValues outputs and pick a favorable one before signing; dice-game (MiniAppDiceGameEVM _settle: rolled = keccak(result) % 6 + 1) trusts it. This is a real trust-model/documentation gap, not an exploitable replay bug, and is partially mitigated by the dstack TEE attestation lane (maybeBuildDstackAttestation binds the TEE quote to output_hash) which constrains remote/external grinding (though not a compromised-enclave/insider). Because the only real residual is "trust the (possibly TEE-attested) signer not to bias, and call this signed randomness rather than an unbiasable VRF," the honest severity is low, not medium.
verified.fix_correction:
The fix's PRIMARY thrust — "build the signed result over {request_id, seed/nonce, randomness, timestamp} to stop cross-request replay" — is largely redundant and would not address a real gap: cross-request/cross-deployment replay is already prevented by the relayer-signed fulfillment digest (MorpheusOracleEVM.fulfillRequest / router.js buildFulfillmentDigestBytes), which binds requestId + deployment + appId/moduleId/operation + result. Adding request_id to the inner worker envelope changes output_hash and would force a coordinated versioned rollout (the fix's own stated Medium risk) for a property already enforced on-chain — net negative.

The fix's SECONDARY point is the correct and safe remediation for the actual residual: either (a) document the lane as "TEE-attested signed randomness," not an unbiasable VRF (cheap, no rollout, accurate), or (b) move to a real ECVRF construction where the on-chain consumer verifies a proof that output is deterministic from (seed, key) — eliminating signer grinding entirely. A pre-commit/seed-binding on the request side (e.g. mix a caller-supplied seed + a value the signer commits before the request, or NeoX block prevrandao) is a lighter-weight bias mitigation than full ECVRF. Recommend (a) immediately and (b)/seed-binding only if unbiasable randomness is a stated requirement for the dice/gaming consumers.

verified.title: deploy_contract_neonjs.mjs computes a wrong predicted contract hash (passes raw hex string where a HexString is required)
verified.reason:
CONFIRMED via code reading + empirical proof. deploy_contract_neonjs.mjs:41-45 passes account.scriptHash to experimental.getContractHash. Account.scriptHash is typed `string` (neon-core Account.d.ts:125). getContractHash's signature requires `sender: u.HexString` (experimental/helpers.d.ts), and its body emits .emitPush(sender). ScriptBuilder.emitPush routes a JS string to emitString (TextEncoder → pushes the 40 ASCII bytes of the hex characters) but routes a HexString to emitHexString (pushes the 20 raw bytes, little-endian). So the current code builds a different script → different hash160 → wrong predicted hash. The finding's quote of neon-js helpers.js:224 is accurate.

EMPIRICAL PROOF (real self-consistent on-chain triple): deployer NR3E4D8N + name MiniAppCoinFlip + on-chain nef.checksum 305546182 → deployed hash 0x238488397884ad0bf1db99aecce62290e9f47971 (confirmed live via getcontractstate on testnet1.neo.coz.io). Running getContractHash with the current raw-string arg yields 0xcde5ab7e... (WRONG); with the proposed fix HexString.fromHex(account.scriptHash) it yields EXACTLY 0x238488397884ad0bf1db99aecce62290e9f47971 (MATCH). This both confirms the bug and validates the fix against authoritative on-chain data. (Note: the local contracts/build NEF has a different checksum 2726112840 than the deployed 305546182, so a naive comparison against the local build would mislead — I used the on-chain checksum.)

The bug is also self-evident from the code's own artifacts: header comment line 99-101, the always-fires note at line 116, and deploy_contract_mainnet.mjs:13 'getContractHash is unreliable' — all symptoms of this misuse, plus the Go path uses state.CreateContractHash as authoritative.

The script is actively used: it is the testnet-pinned deploy tool referenced in the migration plan (claudedocs/remaining-issues-plan-2026-06-13.md) and prior 10 migrations.
verified.fix_correction: The proposed fix `experimental.getContractHash(pkg.u.HexString.fromHex(account.scriptHash), nef.checksum, manifest.name)` is empirically proven correct — it reproduces the exact real deployed hash. pkg.u.HexString.fromHex is confirmed available (the script destructures sc/wallet/rpc/experimental but references pkg.u directly, which works). Default big-endian interpretation is correct because emitHexString internally calls toLittleEndian() to push the canonical 20 raw bytes. Risk is low/safe: one-line change; the authoritative Deploy-notification readback still governs the final RESULT_HASH in the normal path, so the only behavior change is a corrected idempotency precheck and a correct printed expected-hash. The 'alternatively delete the prediction and require a supplied expectedHash' option is also fine (matches deploy_contract_mainnet.mjs).
verified.reason_severity: Downgraded from high to medium. The defect is real but the blast radius is limited: (1) the authoritative ContractManagement Deploy-notification readback (lines 110-119) overrides the wrong prediction, so the final emitted RESULT_HASH is correct in the normal path — no wrong contract hash propagates downstream. (2) The 're-deploy a duplicate' harm is overstated: Neo's ContractManagement.Deploy faults when a contract already exists at that hash, so a silent duplicate cannot occur; the actual consequence is a broken idempotency precheck (the already-deployed skip at line 74-79 never triggers → a wasted/faulted deploy attempt) plus a misleading printed 'expected hash'. (3) This is interactive dev/deploy tooling with operator oversight, not production runtime — no fund loss or user-facing impact. Still worth fixing (trivial, strictly safer), hence medium rather than low.
